cases.case_name: G.V. v. Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: Reversing the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an indicated report of child abuse may be entered and maintained on the statewide ChildLine Registry on the CPSL's legislatively prescribed substantial-evidence standard, and that due process does not require clear and convincing evidence at an expunction hearing.
cases.quote: the proper standard of proof is the legislatively established substantial evidence standard

relevance.INP-01: Fixes the evidentiary consequence of a mandated report: the CPSL's substantial-evidence standard, not a higher one, governs whether the report becomes 'indicated.'
relevance.INP-10: Defines the proof threshold the agency must reach when a screened report is escalated into an investigative finding.
relevance.DEC-01: Supplies the standard that separates an unfounded or screened-out report from an indicated one under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6303.
relevance.DEC-02: Explains what the county agency must be able to prove once it accepts a report for investigation.
relevance.DEC-03: The controlling Pennsylvania rule on the burden and standard of proof supporting a substantiated (indicated) finding and its maintenance on the registry.
relevance.FAIL-01: Shows the limits of judicial reversal of an agency abuse finding: a reviewing court may not raise the statutory standard of proof on its own.
relevance.FAIL-06: Describes the statutory controls limiting who may receive ChildLine information, the frame for any disclosure dispute.
relevance.PMC-05: The court's account of the CPSL's confidentiality and disclosure architecture governs transparency claims about registry data.

cases.case_name: A.Y. v. Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The court reversed the Commonwealth Court and remanded, holding that while hearsay is admissible in a child-abuse expungement hearing, uncorroborated hearsay alone cannot satisfy the agency's burden and the accused is entitled to due process, including consideration of character evidence.
cases.quote: Although less process is due in an administrative proceeding than where criminal charges have been brought, an administrative adjudication of suspected child abuse is of the most serious nature.

relevance.INP-01: Sets the evidentiary weight a reported allegation can carry once it reaches an administrative adjudication.
relevance.INP-02: Governs how much a third-party or relayed account can prove when the agency relies on it.
relevance.DEC-01: An allegation resting only on uncorroborated hearsay cannot support an indicated finding and must be treated as unproven.
relevance.DEC-03: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the quality of evidence required to substantiate abuse against a named perpetrator.
relevance.FAIL-01: Illustrates reversal of an agency finding for reliance on legally insufficient evidence and denial of a fair hearing.

cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating the trial court, the court held that the rebuttable presumption of 23 Pa.C.S. § 6381(d) identifying the caregiver as the abuser applies even where a child was in the care of multiple responsible adults.
cases.quote: when a child is in the care of multiple parents or other persons responsible for care, those individuals are accountable for the care and protection of the child

relevance.INP-01: Explains why injuries reported by treating professionals can, without more, identify the responsible caregiver.
relevance.INP-07: Medical findings of injuries not ordinarily sustained absent abuse are the evidentiary engine of the § 6381(d) presumption.
relevance.DEC-03: Central Pennsylvania authority on identifying the perpetrator for a substantiated finding when several adults had care of the child.
relevance.ACT-06: Treats untreated severe diaper rash and infection as serious physical neglect, framing when medical intervention is required.
relevance.OUT-06: Applies to serious-injury cases where the agency can prove abuse but not who inflicted it.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Superior Court and reinstated the trial court's denial of a goal change, holding that dependency rulings are reviewed only for abuse of discretion and that fifteen months in placement under 42 Pa.C.S. § 6351(f)(9) is one factor, not a litmus test requiring a goal change.
cases.quote: (f)(9) is merely one of a number of factors a trial court must consider in ultimately determining whether the current placement is appropriate

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans are reviewed under the permanency factors of § 6351(f), no one of which is dispositive.
relevance.ACT-03: Governs how a court evaluates whether a child's continued foster placement remains appropriate.
relevance.OUT-01: Confirms that reunification may remain the goal even after long placement if the trial court's findings support it.
relevance.OUT-03: The same § 6351(f) factor analysis controls the choice among permanency options.
relevance.OUT-04: Continued judicial review of placement appropriateness is the vehicle through which older youth remain in care.
relevance.FAIL-03: Rejects a mechanical reading of the ASFA-derived fifteen-of-twenty-two-month provision as a compliance trigger.
relevance.PMC-01: Shows how federal permanency timelines were absorbed into Pennsylvania practice as discretionary factors subject to judicial review.

cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating termination, the court held that an agency's failure to provide reasonable efforts toward reunification does not bar the granting of an otherwise properly proven petition to terminate parental rights, although courts may enforce reasonable efforts by other means.
cases.quote: refusing a properly proven termination of parental rights petition, and thus harming an innocent child, is not among them

relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary and agency-offered services matter, but their absence is remedied by court orders rather than by defeating a termination petition.
relevance.ACT-02: Identifies the remedies a court may use when an agency disobeys service orders, and the one remedy it may not use.
relevance.OUT-01: Marks the point at which reunification ceases to be a realistic goal despite deficient agency efforts.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports front-end service provision while holding that deficiencies in services are addressed by court supervision, not by case outcomes.
relevance.FAIL-03: Holds that a state-law failure to deliver reasonable efforts does not create a defence or private remedy at the termination stage.
relevance.PMC-01: Illustrates the gap between federal reasonable-efforts monitoring and enforceable rights in individual Pennsylvania cases.

cases.holding: The court reversed and ordered termination of parental rights for five siblings, holding that under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(b) an unhealthy or pathological parent-child bond does not preclude termination and that courts must weigh the child's need for permanency and any bond with a pre-adoptive family.
cases.quote: we conclude that severing the parental bond best serves the needs and welfare of these children

relevance.ACT-01: Shows the limit of continued voluntary services where five years of services have not produced parenting capacity.
relevance.ACT-02: Warns that concurrent planning and court-ordered services used beyond their useful life perpetuate foster-care drift.
relevance.ACT-03: The court's discussion of repeated placements frames the harm caused by unstable foster care.
relevance.OUT-01: Identifies when reunification must yield because the parent cannot parent within a reasonable period.
relevance.OUT-02: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare analysis and the weight of parent-child bonds at termination.

cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and reinstating termination, the court held that incarceration is not itself a ground for termination but may be determinative of parental incapacity under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(a)(2), with the length of the remaining sentence highly relevant.
cases.quote: incarceration, while not a litmus test for termination, can be determinative of the question of whether a parent is incapable of providing "essential parental care, control or subsistence"

relevance.ACT-01: Explains how a parent's use of available prison resources and services bears on capacity to resume care.
relevance.OUT-02: The controlling Pennsylvania rule on terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Superior Court, holding that an order compelling a parent to admit child-welfare workers into the home requires probable cause evaluated under ordinary search-and-seizure principles, and that a single stale, uncorroborated anonymous report did not supply it.
cases.quote: We expressly hold that there is no "social worker exception" to compliance with constitutional limitations on an entry into a home without consent or exigent circumstances.

relevance.INP-02: A third-party report is the starting point, not the end point; its veracity and reliability must be assessed before entry is compelled.
relevance.INP-03: Applies the same constitutional limits to child-welfare entries that constrain police searches.
relevance.INP-04: Directly governs the petition-to-compel procedure by which a court orders a family to admit investigators.
relevance.INP-06: Holds that an uncorroborated anonymous hotline report, standing alone, cannot establish probable cause to enter a home.
relevance.INP-08: Requires nexus, source reliability and freshness before any reported observation can justify compelled entry.
relevance.INP-10: The constitutional gate a screened report must pass before the investigation escalates to a compelled home inspection.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines what the agency must show once it accepts a report and seeks court-backed access to the family.
relevance.ACT-06: Allegations of unmet basic needs do not by themselves authorize state entry to verify a child's condition.

cases.holding: The court reversed the Superior Court, holding that a child whose non-custodial parent is ready, willing and able to provide proper care does not meet the Juvenile Act definition of a dependent child and may not be adjudicated dependent.
cases.quote: a child is not dependent if the child has a parent who is willing and able to provide proper care to the child

relevance.INP-04: Where CPS involvement arises inside a private custody dispute, the availability of the other parent defeats dependency.
relevance.INP-05: A guardian's request for intervention cannot produce dependency jurisdiction if that guardian can provide proper care.
relevance.DEC-01: Requires closure without adjudication where an available parent can meet the child's needs.
relevance.DEC-05: Sets the threshold the agency must clear before a dependency petition can succeed.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving cases outside the dependency system where a capable parent is immediately available.
relevance.OUT-01: Placement with the capable non-custodial parent, not dependency, is the correct outcome.
relevance.OUT-05: The controlling ground for dismissal of a dependency petition in Pennsylvania.
relevance.FAIL-01: An appellate reversal of a dependency adjudication entered despite an available, capable parent.

cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded for a hearing on the sixteen-year-old's own wishes, holding that the state's interest does not outweigh a parent's religious objection to surgery where the child's life is not in immediate danger.
cases.quote: the state does not have an interest of sufficient magnitude outweighing a parent's religious beliefs when the child's life is not immediately imperiled by his physical condition

relevance.INP-04: The case arose on an institution's petition to initiate juvenile proceedings, the classic court-ordered referral route.
relevance.INP-05: Addresses state intervention where the parent, not the child, controls the request for or refusal of care.
relevance.INP-07: A treating institution's disclosure of a child's untreated condition triggered the proceeding.
relevance.ACT-06: The leading Pennsylvania authority on when the state may authorize medical treatment over parental objection.

cases.case_name: In re Fortieth Statewide Investigating Grand Jury
cases.holding: The court ordered interim release of the clergy-abuse grand jury report with the challengers' identities redacted, holding that Pennsylvania's constitutional right to reputation requires enhanced procedural protections before a grand jury report publicly condemns named individuals.
cases.quote: the lines between a grand jury "investigation" and an "adjudication" are blurred when the grand jury renders wide-scale, individualized, condemnatory findings

relevance.INP-09: Shows how a statewide investigative body's findings about institutional child abuse are produced and constrained.
relevance.FAIL-06: Balances the public's interest in disclosure of abuse findings against the due-process rights of those named.
relevance.PMC-02: Frames the procedural limits on publishing official findings of institutional wrongdoing.
relevance.PMC-03: Illustrates the process an independent review body must afford before publicly condemning identified actors.
relevance.PMC-04: The Pennsylvania model for a public fatality- or abuse-review report and the process due before release.
relevance.PMC-05: Establishes that redaction, not suppression, is the default remedy when reputation rights collide with public access.
relevance.PMC-06: Sets the constitutional ceiling on publishing individualized accusatory findings drawn from government data.

cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that appellate courts must review sua sponte whether the orphans' court appointed counsel for the child's legal interests under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a), but may not assess sua sponte the quality of that representation or an unraised conflict.
cases.quote: we hold that appellate courts should engage in sua sponte review to determine if orphans' courts have appointed counsel to represent the legal interests of children in contested termination proceedings

relevance.OUT-02: The controlling rule on the child's right to appointed legal counsel in a contested termination and how that right is policed on appeal.

cases.holding: Affirming termination, the court held that a child's statutory right to appointed counsel under 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a) cannot be waived, but that where the child is too young to express a preferred outcome the attorney-guardian ad litem may represent both legal and best interests without conflict.
cases.quote: we hold that a child's statutory right to appointed counsel under Section 2313(a) of the Adoption Act is not subject to waiver

relevance.OUT-02: Defines who must speak for the child at termination and when a single attorney may serve both roles.

cases.holding: The court reversed, holding the evidence insufficient to find the mother a perpetrator of child abuse by omission and that the § 6381(d) presumption does not apply absent evidence the caregiver knew or should have known of the abuse or risk and disregarded it.
cases.quote: we hold there was insufficient evidence to support the juvenile court's finding that Mother was a perpetrator of child abuse under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6303(b.1)

relevance.INP-07: Hospital presentation and medical findings alone did not establish the non-abusing parent's knowledge.
relevance.DEC-01: Where the agency cannot show the caregiver knew or should have known of the risk, the allegation against that caregiver fails.
relevance.DEC-03: The limiting counterpart to In re L.Z.: the caregiver presumption cannot manufacture a substantiated finding by omission.
relevance.OUT-05: Supports vacating a perpetrator finding and closing it out where proof of knowledge is missing.
relevance.FAIL-01: A direct appellate reversal of an agency-sought abuse finding for insufficient evidence.

cases.holding: The court vacated the termination decree and remanded, holding that the en masse admission of 167 agency exhibits without a business-records foundation was an abuse of discretion and that the error was not harmless merely because other admitted evidence could have supported termination.
cases.quote: That there may have been properly admitted evidence sufficient to support termination does not render the orphans' court's substantial evidentiary error harmless.

relevance.DEC-03: Agency case records are not self-proving; each must satisfy the business-records foundation before it can support a finding of abuse or neglect.
relevance.OUT-05: Evidentiary failure by the agency can unwind a completed termination and return the case for rehearing.
relevance.FAIL-01: The leading recent Pennsylvania example of a court reversing an agency-obtained decree for procedural and evidentiary error.

cases.holding: Affirming the Superior Court, the court held that a court-ordered change of the permanency goal is not a condition precedent to an agency's filing of a petition to terminate parental rights, consistent with ASFA's endorsement of concurrent planning.
cases.quote: We conclude that Section 6351 does not require that a goal change precede the filing of a termination petition.

relevance.DEC-05: Establishes the sequencing between dependency permanency review and the filing of a termination petition.
relevance.DEC-06: Concurrent planning allows services to continue while permanency alternatives are pursued, avoiding all-or-nothing tracks.
relevance.ACT-01: Confirms that reunification services continue even after a termination petition is filed.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification can remain the stated goal while the agency pursues an alternative permanency track.
relevance.FAIL-03: Explains how Pennsylvania conformed the Juvenile Act to ASFA's concurrent-planning requirement.
relevance.PMC-01: Traces the federal permanency framework into Pennsylvania's statutory scheme reviewed in the CFSR.

cases.holding: Affirming the Superior Court, the court held that grandparents must be permitted to intervene in the adoption proceedings for their grandchildren, and that an agency's refusal to consent does not control because the court may dispense with an unreasonably withheld agency consent.
cases.quote: A child's interests are best served when all those who demonstrate an interest in his or her welfare are allowed to be heard.

relevance.INP-05: Relatives who come forward after a voluntary relinquishment have a right to be heard rather than be turned away by the agency.
relevance.ACT-04: Foundational Pennsylvania authority that relatives may not be excluded from consideration as caregivers or adoptive resources.
relevance.OUT-03: Establishes that the court, not the agency, decides whether a kinship permanency option serves the child.

cases.holding: The court affirmed adjudications of dependency and findings of aggravated circumstances, holding that clear and convincing evidence of a sibling's severe abuse and of the mother's knowledge supported adjudicating both children dependent.
cases.quote: the trial court was correct in adjudicating L.P. dependent because there was clear and convincing evidence that R.P. was the victim of abuse

relevance.DEC-05: Confirms that a dependency petition may reach a non-injured sibling on proof of abuse to the other child.
relevance.ACT-03: Supports removal and placement of both siblings where severe abuse to one and parental failure to protect are proven.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that an award of permanent legal custody under 42 Pa.C.S. § 6351(a)(2.1) does not terminate parental rights or strip the trial court of jurisdiction to entertain a parent's later petition for primary custody.
cases.quote: Clearly, our legislature did not exclude from parents the right to petition to modify a custody order entered in a dependency proceeding.

relevance.ACT-04: Defines subsidized permanent legal custody, the principal Pennsylvania vehicle for kinship permanency with a relative caregiver.
relevance.OUT-03: The controlling explanation of how permanent legal custody differs from termination and adoption and what rights survive it.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the dependency adjudication of a child certified as a near fatality, holding the trial court did not abuse its discretion where medical evidence established extensive inflicted injuries and the mother failed to seek treatment.
cases.quote: In order to adjudicate a child dependent, the court must determine that the above definition has been met by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.INP-01: A hospital child-abuse team's findings supplied the report and the proof supporting intervention.
relevance.INP-07: Illustrates how a medical encounter documenting inflicted injuries drives the entire child-protection sequence.
relevance.INP-12: Injuries of this severity are the paradigm case for immediate protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Supports emergency removal where medical evidence shows life-threatening inflicted injury and parental failure to obtain care.
relevance.DEC-05: States the clear-and-convincing standard the agency must meet on its dependency petition.
relevance.ACT-03: Supports out-of-home placement where the caregiver continues a relationship with the person who inflicted the injuries.
relevance.OUT-06: A published Pennsylvania decision addressing a formally certified near fatality.
relevance.FAIL-04: Shows the dependency response required when a child suffers near-fatal harm.
relevance.PMC-04: Identifies the 'near fatality' certification that triggers Pennsylvania's mandatory review and disclosure duties.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that 'placement care and responsibility' under the Juvenile Act includes any court-ordered agency supervision of a dependent child, not only cases where the agency holds legal and physical custody, so the youth qualified as having been in placement.
cases.quote: "placement care and responsibility" includes any court-ordered supervision of a dependent child by an agency, not just circumstances where an agency is granted legal and physical custody of a child

relevance.ACT-04: A court-ordered kinship placement with a relative counts as agency placement even without transfer of legal custody.
relevance.OUT-03: Clarifies that kinship permanency arrangements remain within the dependency placement framework.
relevance.OUT-04: The most on-point recent Pennsylvania authority on whether a youth was 'in placement' for purposes of extended foster care and transition benefits.

cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court affirmed termination and held that a parent's claim of ineffective assistance in a termination proceeding is reviewed on direct appeal under a fundamental-fairness standard, with relief only where counsel's failure caused the decree.
cases.quote: Mere assertion of ineffectiveness of counsel is not the basis of a remand or rehearing

relevance.OUT-02: Defines the Pennsylvania right to counsel in involuntary termination and what a parent must show to upset a decree on that ground.
relevance.FAIL-01: Sets the narrow route by which an appellate court will disturb a termination decree for counsel's failures.

cases.holding: The court set aside the termination of an Indian mother's parental rights and ordered the child returned, holding that 25 U.S.C. § 1913(b) of the Indian Child Welfare Act allowed her to withdraw her consent to the foster placement at any time.
cases.quote: appellant had the right and ability to withdraw her consent to the placement and to effect an immediate return of the child

relevance.INP-05: Governs a guardian's voluntary placement of a child and the statutory right to revoke that consent.
relevance.INP-11: The principal published Pennsylvania appellate decision applying the Indian Child Welfare Act, including consent, transfer to tribal court and good cause.
relevance.ACT-04: Shows how ICWA constrains an agency's placement choices for an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Grounds ICWA's protections in the child's political relationship to the tribe rather than in racial classification.

cases.case_name: Egelman ex rel. Egelman v. Egelman
cases.holding: The court reversed and vacated orders that required a bond before filing future protection-from-abuse petitions, confined future child-welfare concerns to the custody docket, and awarded counsel fees, holding that the PFA Act supplies remedies the CPSL and custody process do not.
cases.quote: the Child Protective Service Law (CPSL) and the PFA Act serve different purposes and are not substitute remedies

relevance.DEC-06: Confirms that a family may obtain protection outside the CPS pathway, without a dependency petition.
relevance.ACT-05: The controlling Pennsylvania statement of what a protection-from-abuse order does that the child-protection system cannot, including ex parte relief and exclusion of the abuser.

cases.case_name: Allegheny County Department of Administrative Services v. A Second Chance, Inc.
cases.holding: The court affirmed in part and vacated in part, holding that the Right-to-Know Law's definition of 'record' is not confined to documents the agency itself created or holds, that agency policy bulletins could not create an exemption, and remanding for findings on the contractor's duties.
cases.quote: This language does not limit "record" to only those documents "created, received or retained" by the agency.

relevance.INP-09: Public access to contractor records is a practical oversight lever over privatized child-welfare services.
relevance.FAIL-06: Holds that a county may not shield child-welfare contractor information by pointing to the contractor's private possession or to internal bulletins.
relevance.PMC-02: Supports obtaining the contractor-level records needed to audit spending on kinship and foster services.
relevance.PMC-03: Gives citizen reviewers a statutory route to the operational records of privatized child-welfare providers.
relevance.PMC-05: The leading Pennsylvania RTKL decision on records held by a private child-welfare contractor for a county agency.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the statutory basis for assembling agency and contractor data for independent analysis.

cases.case_name: Support Center for Child Advocates v. Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of the child's guardian ad litem's petition to intervene in the alleged perpetrator's ChildLine expunction appeal, holding the GAL had no statutory right to intervene and no interest not already represented by the Department.
cases.quote: H.M.'s G.A.L. has no right to intervene "conferred by statute," nor has he stated an interest such that his participation "is in the public interest."

relevance.DEC-03: Identifies who may participate when a substantiated finding is challenged administratively: the Department defends the report, not the child's own counsel.
relevance.FAIL-06: Limits third-party access to and participation in the confidential expunction process.
relevance.PMC-05: Shows that even a child's court-appointed advocate has no general right of entry into confidential registry proceedings.

cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children & Youth Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment for the caseworker, the court held that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's substantive due process rights because the caseworker lacked objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
cases.quote: we hold that she lacked objectively reasonable grounds to believe the child had been sexually abused or was in imminent danger of sexual abuse

relevance.INP-02: A third-party allegation must be corroborated before it can justify coercive interference with the family.
relevance.INP-03: Sets the threshold of suspicion that any child-protection actor must reach before disrupting a family.
relevance.INP-06: The controlling Third Circuit holding that an anonymous, uncorroborated tip does not justify state interference with custody.
relevance.INP-08: Requires objectively reasonable grounds regardless of who reported the suspicion.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the constitutional line between investigating a report and acting coercively on it.
relevance.INP-12: Protective action requires reasonable and articulable evidence of abuse or imminent danger.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigation may proceed on a tip, but coercive measures may not without objective corroboration.
relevance.DEC-04: The governing Third Circuit standard for the constitutionality of an emergency separation decision.
relevance.ACT-05: Treats a caseworker's ultimatum that a parent leave the home as a coercive deprivation requiring justification.
relevance.FAIL-02: Binding circuit authority for § 1983 liability where a family is separated without objectively reasonable grounds.

cases.case_name: Good v. Dauphin County Social Services for Children & Youth
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment on qualified immunity, holding that on the mother's version of the facts a caseworker and police officer entered the home and strip-searched the child without valid consent, a warrant, or exigent circumstances, violating clearly established law.
cases.quote: under these circumstances a reasonable law enforcement officer could not have believed Ms. Good had given legally effective consent to either the entry or the subsequent strip search

relevance.INP-02: A single anonymous report of unspecified bruises did not justify forced entry or a body search.
relevance.INP-03: The leading Third Circuit case on a joint caseworker-police home entry in a child-abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-06: Holds that an anonymous hotline report alone does not create an emergency justifying warrantless entry.
relevance.INP-08: Applies the same Fourth Amendment limits to investigative body searches of children whatever the report's source.
relevance.INP-10: Consent obtained by asserting that no warrant is needed is not consent, and cannot authorize escalation.
relevance.INP-12: Defines the emergency exception: imminent danger of serious bodily injury with intrusion reasonably necessary to avert it.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets the constitutional constraints on investigative techniques once a report is accepted.
relevance.DEC-04: The removal-adjacent investigative intrusion must be justified by consent, warrant, or true exigency.
relevance.ACT-05: Illustrates that protective measures imposed under claim of authority without process are unconstitutional.
relevance.FAIL-02: Foundational Third Circuit authority on § 1983 liability for unlawful entry and search in a child-protection investigation.

cases.case_name: Ernst v. Child & Youth Services of Chester County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed judgment for the agency defendants on absolute-immunity grounds, holding that child-welfare workers act in a quasi-prosecutorial capacity when they prepare for, initiate and prosecute dependency proceedings and are absolutely immune from § 1983 damages for those acts.
cases.quote: we hold that the CYS defendants are entitled to absolute immunity for their actions on behalf of the state in preparing for, initiating, and prosecuting dependency proceedings

relevance.DEC-05: Filing and prosecuting the dependency petition is a quasi-prosecutorial function, immunized from damages suits.
relevance.FAIL-02: Marks the boundary of § 1983 remedies: investigative conduct may be actionable, but petition-stage conduct is absolutely immune.
relevance.FAIL-04: Limits damages liability of caseworkers for harms flowing from court-directed dependency outcomes.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers' ex parte presentations to the judge that stripped the mother of custody violated procedural due process, but that the individual caseworkers were absolutely immune, and remanded for trial on the county's liability.
cases.quote: We agree with Mother that her procedural due process rights were violated by the Appellees, though the individual defendants are protected by absolute immunity.

relevance.INP-03: Coordination among agency staff and the court cannot substitute for notice and an opportunity to be heard.
relevance.INP-04: Governs how a court-issued custody order obtained on an agency's ex parte presentation is reviewed constitutionally.
relevance.INP-12: Distinguishes genuine emergencies, where ex parte action may be tolerated, from non-emergency ex parte contacts.
relevance.DEC-04: Holds that a non-emergency removal obtained ex parte violates procedural due process.
relevance.FAIL-02: The controlling Third Circuit case on municipal liability for a custom of removing children through ex parte judicial contacts.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held that placing a child in state-regulated foster care creates a special relationship imposing affirmative constitutional duties, but affirmed summary judgment because the caseworker's conduct amounted at most to negligence and did not shock the conscience.
cases.quote: when the state places a child in state-regulated foster care, the state has entered into a special relationship with that child which imposes upon it certain affirmative duties

relevance.ACT-03: Establishes the constitutional duties the state assumes the moment it places a child in foster care.
relevance.OUT-04: Applies to older youth placed with informal or para-foster caregivers as they move toward adulthood.
relevance.OUT-06: Sets the culpability standard for constitutional claims when a child is harmed while in care.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines the affirmative duty that attaches once removal has occurred, alongside the limits on removal itself.
relevance.FAIL-04: The governing Third Circuit standard for liability when a child is injured or dies in state-arranged placement.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why deaths and serious injuries in care raise constitutional, not merely administrative, questions.

cases.case_name: Bayer v. Monroe County Children & Youth Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that even assuming a constitutional right to a post-removal hearing within seventy-two hours, that right was not clearly established such that the Pennsylvania caseworkers' conduct was objectively unreasonable.
cases.quote: we consider it objectively reasonable for defendants to have believed, under the law existing at the time, that their particular conduct in this case was lawful

relevance.INP-12: Addresses the timing of the post-custody hearing that must follow a Pennsylvania protective-custody seizure.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows how delay between an emergency removal and the shelter-care hearing is analysed constitutionally.
relevance.FAIL-02: A realistic assessment of qualified immunity for Pennsylvania caseworkers sued over removal and post-removal delay.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court vacated and remanded, holding that before a State may irrevocably sever the parent-child relationship the Due Process Clause requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, so a preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
cases.quote: the "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard prescribed by Fam. Ct. Act § 622 violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

relevance.OUT-02: The federal constitutional floor for the standard of proof in every Pennsylvania involuntary termination case.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that the 'reasonable efforts' state-plan requirement of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), confers no privately enforceable right and cannot be sued upon under § 1983 or an implied right of action.
cases.quote: the "reasonable efforts" language does not unambiguously confer an enforceable right upon the Act's beneficiaries

relevance.INP-09: Places enforcement of the federal plan requirements with the Secretary, which is why administrative review and audit are the operative oversight tools.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered services rest on state law; the federal reasonable-efforts clause gives families no independent claim.
relevance.FAIL-03: The controlling authority that federal child-welfare plan failures are remedied through funding oversight, not private litigation.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why the CFSR and the Secretary's funding leverage, rather than lawsuits, drive federal performance monitoring.
relevance.PMC-02: Confirms that fiscal and program audit is the designated federal enforcement mechanism.
relevance.PMC-03: Underscores that citizen review operates outside any privately enforceable federal right.
relevance.PMC-06: Sets the legal ceiling on what citizen-driven analysis of federal noncompliance can compel in court.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative constitutional duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence where the child remains in the parent's custody rather than in state custody.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.INP-09: Explains why systemic accountability for agency inaction runs through oversight and state law rather than federal constitutional claims.
relevance.OUT-06: The threshold rule for constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or seriously injured at home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Distinguishes children harmed in the home, who have no constitutional protection claim, from children the state has taken into custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Frames why fatality review is a policy and oversight function, not a constitutional remedy.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the limit of constitutional accountability for failures to intervene that citizen analysis may surface.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Reversing the Third Circuit, the Court held that Philadelphia's refusal to contract with a religious foster agency unless it certified same-sex couples burdened free exercise and failed strict scrutiny because the city's contract allowed individualized exemptions.
cases.quote: The refusal of Philadelphia to contract with CSS for the provision of foster care services unless it agrees to certify same-sex couples as foster parents cannot survive strict scrutiny

relevance.FAIL-05: The controlling decision, arising from Philadelphia's own foster-care system, on when nondiscrimination requirements imposed on placement agencies violate the Free Exercise Clause.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's authority to enact it and rejecting the anticommandeering claims on the merits while dismissing the equal-protection and nondelegation claims for lack of standing.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute

relevance.INP-11: Confirms that ICWA's placement preferences and procedures remain binding on Pennsylvania courts in cases involving Indian children.
relevance.FAIL-05: Leaves ICWA's preferences intact while resolving the racial-discrimination challenge only on standing, so the equal-protection question is undecided.

cases.holding: Vacating the orders below and remanding, the court held that a 23 Pa.C.S. § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare analysis may not stop at evidence of an emotional or adverse-impact bond but must determine whether the parental bond is necessary and beneficial and must also weigh the child's need for permanency, stability and any bond with a pre-adoptive family.
cases.quote: Therefore, to grant termination when a parental bond exists, there must be clear and convincing evidence that the bond is not necessary and beneficial.

relevance.OUT-02: The controlling modern Pennsylvania statement of the § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare and bond analysis, decided a decade after T.S.M. and correcting the truncated reading lower courts had drawn from it.
relevance.ACT-03: Requires the court to weigh the child's bond with the pre-adoptive foster family and the stability of that placement before severing the parental bond.

cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and remanding with instructions to reinstate the trial court's order, the court held that the Superior Court exceeded its scope of review in rejecting supported findings that the father's alcoholism was an obstacle he overcame with reasonable firmness, and that the petitioners proved neither § 2511(a)(1) nor § 2511(a)(2) by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: In recognition of the gravity attendant to the termination of parental rights, the moving party must establish the statutory grounds by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Leading Pennsylvania authority on the § 2511(a)(1) abandonment ground, the petitioner's clear-and-convincing burden, and the deference an appellate court owes the trial court's findings on parental duties.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows how a termination petition properly fails, and the parent's rights survive, where the petitioner cannot carry the statutory burden on any ground.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Affirming in part and reversing in part, the Court held that due process entitles a criminal defendant to have Pennsylvania's confidential CYS child-abuse file reviewed in camera by the trial court for material exculpatory evidence, but does not entitle defense counsel to search the file itself.
cases.quote: Although we recognize that the public interest in protecting this type of sensitive information is strong, we do not agree that this interest necessarily prevents disclosure in all circumstances.

relevance.FAIL-06: The governing decision on when Pennsylvania's confidentiality of CYS child-abuse records must yield to a competing constitutional right of access, and on the in camera mechanism for resolving that clash.
relevance.PMC-05: Holds that a confidentiality scheme which itself contemplates court-ordered disclosure is not an absolute bar, so access disputes are resolved by judicial review rather than by agency refusal.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment for the city and its caseworker, the court held that procedural due process does not require a parent's participation in an emergency ex parte custody hearing, and that a social worker's conduct in separating parent and child violates substantive due process only where it exceeds negligence and deliberate indifference and reaches gross negligence or arbitrariness that shocks the conscience.
cases.quote: the standard of culpability for substantive due process purposes must exceed both negligence and deliberate indifference, and reach a level of gross negligence or arbitrariness that indeed "shocks the conscience."

relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the Third Circuit's culpability standard for judging an emergency removal decision and holds a parent need not be heard before an ex parte custody order issues.
relevance.FAIL-02: The circuit's controlling articulation of the 'shocks the conscience' threshold a § 1983 removal claim must clear, and the frame in which Croft and B.S. are applied.
relevance.INP-12: Explains why the protective-custody process may proceed ex parte without building in a pre-deprivation hearing whenever a parent happens to be available.

cases.case_name: In re Petition to Compel Cooperation with Child Abuse Investigation
cases.holding: Vacating the order compelling parents to admit caseworkers, the court held that the CPSL and its mandatory home-visit regulation are subject to the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8, so a petition to compel must allege facts amounting to probable cause, which a bare ChildLine referral of possible medical neglect did not.
cases.quote: if a home visit is refused and C & Y is unable to determine whether conditions in the home present a risk to the child, it must petition the court

relevance.INP-04: The binding panel decision that first defined the petition-to-compel procedure by which a court orders a family to admit investigators, and the authority Y.W.-B. later states it agrees with.
relevance.INP-06: Holds that a ChildLine referral of possible neglect, without more, cannot support an order compelling entry into the home.
relevance.INP-10: Marks the constitutional gate between an accepted report and a court-backed escalation to a compelled home inspection.
relevance.DEC-02: Defines what a county agency must plead once it accepts a report and seeks judicial compulsion of the family's cooperation.

cases.case_name: R. v. Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: Affirming the Commonwealth Court, the court held that an alleged perpetrator was not denied due process at a ChildLine expunction hearing where the hearing examiner who decided the case had not observed all the witnesses and the child testified in camera subject to cross-examination, because the CPSL narrowly limits who may learn of an indicated report.
cases.quote: we conclude that R. received all the process he was due under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution

relevance.DEC-03: The Supreme Court's earlier construction of the process due when an indicated report resting on substantial evidence is challenged, and necessary background to G.V.
relevance.FAIL-06: Grounds the constitutionality of the indicated-report scheme in the statute's narrow limits on who may receive registry information.
relevance.PMC-05: Explains why the CPSL's restrictions on disclosure of an indicated report survive constitutional scrutiny, setting the baseline against which transparency claims are measured.

cases.case_name: Mulholland v. Government County of Berks, Pennsylvania
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming judgment as a matter of law for the county, the court held that the CPSL's appeal process supplies all the process due to a person listed as an indicated perpetrator, so a county policy of not forwarding exculpatory information to ChildLine is not a constitutional violation, and that the removal rested on objectively reasonable suspicion.
cases.quote: That standard is met if the child is removed without "an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse," based on the information available at the time.

relevance.DEC-04: States when a removal decision crosses into conscience-shocking territory and applies that test to a Pennsylvania county agency's decision to petition for removal.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that an unrebutted ChildLine listing can supply the reasonable suspicion needed to take children into care from the listed perpetrator's household.
relevance.FAIL-06: Rejects a constitutional duty on a county agency to forward recantations and other exculpatory information to the statewide registry after its investigation closes, leaving correction to the CPSL appeal.

cases.holding: Reversing the Superior Court and remanding for a new termination proceeding, the court held that 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a) requires appointment of counsel to serve the child's legal interests in a contested involuntary termination, and that the failure to appoint such counsel is structural error not subject to harmless-error analysis.
cases.quote: we hold that Section 2313(a) requires the appointment of counsel who serves the child's legal interests in contested, involuntary TPR proceedings.

relevance.OUT-02: The origin of the § 2313(a) separate-counsel and structural-error rule that In re T.S. and In re Adoption of K.M.G. build on; Parts I, II(A) and II(C), which contain both holdings, are the Opinion of the Court even though Part II(B) commanded only a plurality.

cases.case_name: Heinrich v. Conemaugh Valley Memorial Hospital
cases.holding: Affirming dismissal on preliminary objections, the court held that hospital staff and physicians who reported suspected child abuse were immune under 23 Pa.C.S. § 6318 because general averments of malice failed to plead the specific facts needed to rebut the statutory presumption of a reporter's good faith.
cases.quote: We cannot fault Appellees, given the criminal penalty imposed for failing to report suspected child abuse, from making a report under these circumstances.

relevance.INP-01: The published Pennsylvania authority on a mandated reporter's own exposure: § 6318 immunity attaches to the act of reporting and the presumption of good faith must be rebutted with specific facts.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that the immunity and good-faith presumption protect the report itself, whatever its ultimate accuracy, so long as bad faith is not specifically pleaded.
relevance.INP-07: An emergency-room presentation of unexplained swelling in a seven-month-old was enough to make the medical report a good-faith one as a matter of law.
relevance.INP-08: Sets out the § 6311(b) roster of mandated reporters, which expressly includes school administrators, teachers and school nurses, and the same immunity they share with medical reporters.

cases.holding: Reversing summary judgment and remanding, the court held that although the CPSL creates no private cause of action for failure to report suspected child abuse, a child may pursue an ordinary medical-malpractice claim where expert testimony would let a jury find that the physicians' standard of care required them to recognize and report the abuse.
cases.quote: the CPSL does not expressly preclude civil liability for a failure to report abuse, nor immunize those who fail in their reporting obligations

relevance.INP-01: The leading Pennsylvania decision on the consequences of not reporting: no CPSL cause of action, but the reporting obligation can form part of a professional's common-law standard of care.
relevance.INP-07: Treats a series of physicians' failures to recognize and report inflicted fractures as an ordinary question of medical malpractice for the jury.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the Pennsylvania route to civil accountability where a child is catastrophically injured after professionals failed to report, the CPSL itself furnishing no remedy.

notes: Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener during this session and its majority opinion text was read; all quotes were programmatically verified as exact substrings of the retrieved opinion text after whitespace and quotation-mark normalization. No case was included from memory.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries across the PA files are keyword-matched noise — per curiam rules orders, attorney-discipline orders, judicial-appointment orders and bare allocatur listings, with synthetic citations. None were retained. Two titles there ('In Re: Adoption of: L.A.K.' and 'In Re: Adoption of: A.L.K.') point to a real 2021 Pa. Supreme Court termination case, but CourtListener carries only the responsive concurring/dissenting filings ([MO: Donohue, J.]) as separate clusters for those dockets, so no majority text could be quoted and the case was excluded.

CORRECTION to the note above (this pass): that statement was wrong. CourtListener cluster 5311739 (opinion 5140281) carries the full 69,000-character majority Opinion by Justice Donohue in In re Adoption of L.A.K. / In re Adoption of A.L.K. It was retrieved and read in this session, and the case has been added.

Gap — mandated-reporter duty and immunity. PARTIALLY CLOSED this pass. Two published Superior Court decisions construing the reporting provisions were located and added: Heinrich v. Conemaugh Valley Memorial Hospital (23 Pa.C.S. § 6318 immunity and the § 6318(b) presumption of good faith) and K.H. v. Kumar (no private cause of action under the CPSL for failure to report, but a common-law malpractice claim may lie). No published Pennsylvania appellate decision construing § 6319 (the summary/misdemeanor offence of willful failure to report) as a stand-alone prosecution surfaced in this session's searches; the offence is quoted in Heinrich's footnote 1 but not litigated there.

Gap — educational disclosure (INP-08). Still open. A targeted CourtListener search for a published Pennsylvania decision on school-staff reporting (pa, pasuperct, pacommwct) returned zero results. INP-08 is now carried by Y.W.-B., Croft and Good (which state the constitutional limits on the agency's response whatever the source of the report) plus Heinrich, which sets out the § 6311(b) roster of mandated reporters expressly including school administrators, teachers and school nurses and applies the same § 6318 immunity to them. None is a school-reporter case on its facts.

Gap — differential/alternative response (DEC-06). Pennsylvania has no appellate case law on 'differential response' as such. The node is carried by In re M.L. (no dependency adjudication where a capable non-custodial parent is available) and Egelman (the PFA Act as a distinct non-CPSL protective route), plus the concurrent-planning cases.

Gap — children missing from care. No Pennsylvania or Third Circuit published decision on children who go missing from foster placement was found. OUT-06 and FAIL-04 rest on Nicini (affirmative duties once the state places a child) and DeShaney (no duty where the child remains at home), plus K.H. v. Kumar for the failure-to-report pathway to serious injury.

Gap — federal compliance and oversight nodes (FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03, PMC-06). There is no Pennsylvania case law on CFSR performance, Single Audit findings, or Citizen Review Panels. These nodes are carried by the governing federal standard, Suter v. Artist M., which holds that the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' plan requirement is enforced by the Secretary through funding, not by private suit. In re Fortieth Statewide Investigating Grand Jury and Allegheny County v. A Second Chance are included because they are the closest Pennsylvania authority on how official findings are published and how contractor records are obtained.

Statutory-vintage caution. G.V. (2014), A.Y. (1994) and R. v. Department of Public Welfare (1994) construe the Child Protective Services Law as it stood before the 2013-14 reform package substantially rewrote 23 Pa.C.S. § 6303 and related provisions. The substantial-evidence standard G.V. upholds is the standard the General Assembly set, but the operative definitions of 'child abuse' and 'perpetrator' changed; confirm the version of the statute in force for the conduct at issue. In re L.Z. itself flags the amended definition in a footnote. Heinrich (1994) likewise quotes the pre-amendment text of §§ 6311 and 6318.

Citation form. Five Pennsylvania Supreme Court decisions in this brief (In the Interest of Y.W.-B., In re Adoption of K.M.G., In the Interest of N.B.-A., In the Interest of K.T., In re Adoption of L.A.K.) are carried in CourtListener only as slip opinions, with no reporter citation in the cluster record; they are given in slip form with docket numbers taken from the opinion caption. In the Interest of S.K. is published but carries only the public-domain citation 2025 Pa. Super. 22 in CourtListener.

Court metadata. CourtListener's search index labels the Harvard-imported clusters for In re Adoption of T.M.F. and In re Adoption of K.L.R.F. with court_id 'pa', but both are Superior Court decisions (392 Pa. Super. 598; 356 Pa. Super. 555). court_id is reported here as 'pasuperct' to match the reporter and the opinion caption. For K.L.R.F. the CourtListener cluster date_filed is 1987-02-24 (the reargument-denied date); the opinion itself states it was filed September 8, 1986, which is the date given here.

Third Circuit cases. Nicini v. Morra arose in New Jersey but is binding circuit precedent in Pennsylvania federal courts. Croft, Good, Ernst, B.S., Bayer, Miller v. City of Philadelphia and Mulholland all arise from Pennsylvania county agencies or the Philadelphia DHS.

Child's counsel in termination. In re Adoption of L.B.M. is now included. Its Part II(B) (whether a GAL may serve as the child's counsel) commanded only a plurality, but Justice Wecht delivered the Opinion of the Court with respect to Part I, Part II(A) and Part II(C); the quote and holding given here come from II(A) and II(C), which are majority holdings. In re T.S. and In re Adoption of K.M.G. remain the later refinements (non-waivable right; attorney-GAL may serve both roles for a pre-verbal child; sua sponte appellate review of appointment only).

Excluded on quality grounds. Appeal of Miller v. Berks County Children & Youth Services, 465 A.2d 614 (Pa. 1983) (race and sibling considerations in placement) was retrieved and read but is an Opinion Announcing the Judgment of the Court with no majority, so it was not used. Department of Public Welfare v. Eiseman, 125 A.3d 19 (Pa. 2015) was retrieved but concerns Medicaid managed-care rates rather than child welfare, and A Second Chance covers the same Right-to-Know ground on child-welfare facts. Matter of Cabrera, 552 A.2d 1114 (Pa. Super. 1989) was read in the prior pass but its holding sentence could not be quoted within the 30-word limit without dropping a qualifying condition, and a renewed search of pasuperct in this session did not return the cluster; Green Appeal therefore continues to carry the medical-treatment rule, now joined at ACT-06 by Y.W.-B. and In re L.Z.
No unpublished or non-precedential decisions were used. Every case listed is a published/precedential opinion in CourtListener.

Added In the Interest of K.T., No. 37 WAP 2022 (Pa. June 21, 2023) (cluster 9408001) for OUT-02 and ACT-03: the Supreme Court's controlling modern treatment of the § 2511(b) needs-and-welfare and bond analysis, holding that a court may not refuse termination on evidence of an adverse impact alone but must find the bond necessary and beneficial while weighing permanency and the pre-adoptive placement. Note on cluster identity: the two clusters the verifier named, 9408002 and 9408004, both carry only Justice Wecht's dissenting opinion (header '[MO: Dougherty, J.]'). The majority Opinion by Justice Dougherty is in clusters 9408001 and 9408003 (opinions 9403477 and 9403479, identical text); cluster 9408001 is cited here.

Added In re Adoption of L.A.K., No. 14 WAP 2021 (Pa. Dec. 23, 2021) (cluster 5311739) for OUT-02 and OUT-05: leading authority on the § 2511(a)(1) abandonment ground, the petitioner's clear-and-convincing burden, and the limits of appellate review of a trial court's finding that a parent acted with reasonable firmness in overcoming an obstacle such as addiction. It was mapped to OUT-05 rather than FAIL-01 because the reversal was of an intermediate appellate court in a private stepparent termination, not of a child-welfare agency decision, and because FAIL-01 already carries six authorities.

Added Pennsylvania v. Ritchie, 480 U.S. 39 (1987) (cluster 111822) for FAIL-06 and PMC-05: arising from Pennsylvania's own CPSL and a county CYS file, it is the governing authority on when confidential child-abuse agency records must be disclosed and on in camera review as the mechanism for resolving confidentiality against a competing right of access. The quote is taken from Part III-B, which Justice Powell delivered as the Opinion of the Court (Part III-A, the Confrontation Clause discussion, is a plurality and was not used).

Added Miller v. City of Philadelphia, 174 F.3d 368 (3d Cir. 1999) (cluster 763470) for DEC-04, FAIL-02 and INP-12: the circuit's governing articulation of the culpability standard for caseworker conduct in seeking a child's removal, and the source of the 'exceed both negligence and deliberate indifference' formulation that Mulholland and B.S. later apply.

Added In re Petition to Compel Cooperation with Child Abuse Investigation, 875 A.2d 365 (Pa. Super. 2005) (cluster 1475317) for INP-04, INP-06, INP-10 and DEC-02: the binding panel decision holding the CPSL and its mandatory home-visit regulation subject to the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 8, requiring a verified petition alleging probable cause, and the decision Y.W.-B. states its holding is in agreement with.

Added R. v. Department of Public Welfare, 535 Pa. 440, 636 A.2d 142 (1994) (cluster 2207723) for DEC-03, FAIL-06 and PMC-05: the Supreme Court's earlier treatment of what process is due at a ChildLine expunction hearing on an indicated report, resting on the narrowness of the CPSL's permitted disclosures; it is the necessary context for G.V. and for this brief's statutory-vintage caveat.

Added Mulholland v. Government County of Berks, 706 F.3d 227 (3d Cir. 2013) (cluster 816127) for DEC-04, INP-12 and FAIL-06: a Pennsylvania child-removal and ChildLine case holding that the CPSL appeal process supplies all the process due to an indicated perpetrator, that no constitutional duty requires a county to forward exculpatory information to the registry, and that an unrebutted ChildLine listing supported objectively reasonable suspicion for removal. It was mapped to FAIL-06 rather than FAIL-02 because FAIL-02 already carries six authorities and the exculpatory-update holding is the most distinctive contribution.

Added In re Adoption of L.B.M., 161 A.3d 172, 639 Pa. 428 (2017) (cluster 4378735) for OUT-02: the origin of the § 2313(a) separate-counsel and structural-error rule on which In re T.S. and In re Adoption of K.M.G. build. The prior pass excluded it as a plurality; that is correct only as to Part II(B). Parts I, II(A) and II(C) are the Opinion of the Court and contain both holdings relied on here.

Added Heinrich v. Conemaugh Valley Memorial Hospital, 648 A.2d 53, 436 Pa. Super. 465 (1994) (cluster 1523464) for INP-01, INP-02, INP-07 and INP-08: the published Pennsylvania authority on 23 Pa.C.S. § 6318 reporter immunity and the presumption of good faith, closing part of the mandated-reporter gap the prior pass flagged as unlitigated.

Added K.H. v. Kumar, 122 A.3d 1080 (Pa. Super. 2015) (cluster 2830539) for INP-01, INP-07 and FAIL-04: holds that the CPSL creates no private cause of action for failure to report suspected child abuse, but that a child may pursue an ordinary medical-malpractice claim where expert testimony would let a jury find the standard of care required the professional to recognise and report the abuse.

node_map repairs. Three nodes had fewer than two cases in the reconciled brief only because existing case entries whose relevance objects already addressed those nodes had not been listed in node_map. Those mappings are now recorded, with no change to any case entry: INP-03 gains Croft (732428) and B.S. (814981); INP-08 gains Y.W.-B. (5311733), Croft (732428) and Good (533797); ACT-06 gains Y.W.-B. (5311733) and In re L.Z. (2789257). Every one of the 42 nodes now carries at least two authorities.

Deviation from the 2-6 per node guideline. OUT-02 (termination of parental rights / adoption) now carries nine authorities. Pennsylvania's termination law splits into three separate lines that a practitioner needs together - the grounds and burden under § 2511(a) (L.A.K., S.P.), the needs-and-welfare and bond analysis under § 2511(b) (K.T., T.S.M., with Santosky as the federal proof floor), and the child's and parent's right to counsel (L.B.M., In re T.S., K.M.G., T.M.F.). No existing entry could be removed from OUT-02 without leaving verified authority unmapped, and all three additions at this node were identified by the verifier as leading precedent. Every other node is within the 2-6 range.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of C.M., 255 A.3d 343 (Pa. 2021) — the Supreme Court's controlling restatement of the § 2511(a)(1) parental-duties analysis and the clear-and-convincing burden. Both In re K.T. and In re Adoption of L.A.K., which the brief does include, treat C.M. as the governing authority and quote it for the standard (the L.A.K. quote the brief relies on is itself a quotation of C.M., 255 A.3d at 358). A practitioner reading OUT-02 will be sent to C.M. by every case in the node and will not find it there.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Adoption of Charles E.D.M., II, 708 A.2d 88 (Pa. 1998) — the canonical Pennsylvania formulation of 'clear, direct, weighty and convincing' evidence in involuntary termination, and the source C.M. and L.A.K. both cite for it. It is the PA-law counterpart to Santosky's federal floor at OUT-02, which currently has no PA case stating the standard in its own terms.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the Supreme Court's holding that due process does not categorically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in a termination proceeding, with case-by-case determination. OUT-02 carries an elaborate treatment of the CHILD's right to counsel (L.B.M., T.S., K.M.G.) and only In re Adoption of T.M.F. on the parent's side; Lassiter is the constitutional baseline against which Pennsylvania's broader statutory right to parental counsel (42 Pa.C.S. § 6337; 23 Pa.C.S. § 2313(a.1)) operates, and its absence leaves the parent-counsel line of the node without a foundation.

Missing (for a later pass): Commonwealth v. Lynn, 114 A.3d 796 (Pa. 2015) — the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania's decision that a supervisory official who is not the child's direct caregiver may be convicted of endangering the welfare of children under 18 Pa.C.S. § 4304. It is the leading Pennsylvania authority on institutional and supervisory failure to protect children from a known abuser, and is directly relevant to INP-01 (consequences of non-reporting by professionals), INP-09 (institutional investigations) and FAIL-04. The brief flags an unclosed gap on the criminal consequences of failing to act on suspected abuse; Lynn is the closest Pennsylvania Supreme Court authority in that space.

Missing (for a later pass): Mammaro v. New Jersey Division of Child Protection & Permanency, 814 F.3d 164 (3d Cir. 2016) — binding Third Circuit authority holding that the right to familial integrity was not clearly established so as to defeat qualified immunity for a temporary removal, and that temporary removals are analyzed differently from the permanent separations in Croft. It is the most recent circuit word on qualified immunity in removal cases and materially qualifies how Croft, B.S. and Miller are applied at DEC-04, INP-12 and FAIL-02, all of which currently present pre-2013 authority as the operative law.
